query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, an optimal degree of lattice distortion—driven by atomic-size mismatches—suppresses the enthalpy‐driven ordering that otherwise promotes secondary phase formation at low temperatures, thereby stabilizing a single-phase disordered structure that retains high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy in a predominantly single-phase solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Vary the relative concentration of aluminum (or another element with a distinct atomic radius) systematically to modify the lattice distortion magnitude.
generation.conditions: Samples are synthesized under identical processing conditions and subjected to a wide temperature range tests, from cryogenic to high temperatures, with environmental and radiation exposure tests as relevant.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion resulting from atomic-size mismatches among the constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: A sufficient lattice distortion increases the activation barrier for ordering phenomena and the formation of detrimental secondary phases. The high configurational entropy at elevated temperatures further stabilizes the single-phase disordered state, ensuring that the desired mechanical and environmental properties are retained across extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy variants with a controlled increase in atomic-size mismatch (up to a critical threshold) will exhibit enhanced phase stability (i.e., remain single-phase) and improved combinations of high-temperature strength, resistance to corrosion and radiation, and toughness at cryogenic temperatures compared to a baseline composition.
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy composition under similar processing and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for compositions where the atomic-size mismatch is moderate. Excessive mismatch may lead to overly high strains causing brittleness or the direct precipitation of secondary phases, thereby violating the single-phase condition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical threshold of lattice distortion that optimally balances entropic stabilization and the suppression of ordering enthalpy is not precisely known and may depend on processing conditions and minor compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with incremental increases in Al (or another appropriate element) to modulate the atomic-size mismatch. Process all samples under the same conditions and then conduct heat treatments across relevant temperature ranges while also offering controlled radiation and environmental exposure tests. Employ X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to assess phase composition and lattice distortion, and perform mechanical tests at cryogenic and high temperatures.
measurements: Quantitative X-ray diffraction for lattice parameters and phase identification
Electron microscopy for microstructural evidence of secondary phase precipitates
Mechanical testing (tensile, yield strength, toughness) across varied temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with increased lattice distortion (via modified Al content) do not display a statistically significant delay or suppression in the formation of secondary phases and show no corresponding improvement in the targeted properties relative to the baseline composition, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion is the key mediator for phase stability in these alloys would be falsified.

They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
